n: Bildad, the second friend, speaks again. His second speech is short, stinging, and entirely about the fate of the wicked.

f.g: Possibly a descendant of Shuah, a son of Abraham and Keturah.

n: Bildad tells Job to stop talking and think, so a real conversation can happen.
He is offended that Job treats the friends as dumb animals and considers them stupid.
Bildad says Job is tearing himself apart in anger. Does Job expect the whole world order to be rearranged just for him?

f.w: shall the rock be removed out of his place?
f.g: Will God change the fixed moral laws of the universe for your sake?

n: Bildad’s main point: the light of the wicked always goes out. Their life and success are snuffed like a fire.

f.w: light of the wicked shall be put out

n: The lamp in the wicked man’s tent grows dark — a picture of a household and family line coming to an end.

f.g: Lamp. A burning lamp in a home was a sign of life and continuing family.

n: His once-strong stride is cut short, and his own scheming brings him down.
Bildad piles up hunting images: the wicked man walks into his own net and treads on a trap.

f.w: cast into a net by his own feet

n: A trap snaps on his heel and holds him tight.
A noose is hidden in the ground and a trap on his path. Bildad uses six words for traps in verses 8–10 to stress that escape is impossible.

f.g: A hidden noose or cord trap.

n: Terrors surround him and chase him at every step.
His strength is starved away, and disaster stands ready beside him.
Disease eats away his skin and limbs. The “firstborn of death” is a vivid name for the deadliest disease — an unmistakable jab at Job’s own illness.

f.g: A poetic name for a deadly plague or disease.

n: He is torn from the security of his home and marched off to the “king of terrors” — death itself.

f.g: Death, personified as a ruler of the underworld.

n: Strangers will live in his tent, and burning sulfur will be scattered on his home, as at Sodom.

f.g: Burning sulfur, a sign of total judgment.

n: Like a tree, he withers from the roots up and his branches are cut off.

f.w: His roots shall be dried up

n: No one will remember him; his name will vanish from public life.
He will be driven from light into darkness and expelled from the world of the living.

f.g: Banished from the land of the living.

n: He will have no children or descendants left — a cruel jab, since Job’s children have died.

f.g: Nephew here means grandson or descendant.

n: People in the west and east alike will be horrified at his fate.

f.g: Possibly “those in the west … those in the east” — everyone everywhere.

n: Bildad’s conclusion: this is the fate of those who do not know God. He implies Job is one of them — but chapter 1 says otherwise.
